idiom_name: companion object apply / from with Either
implementation_notes: Scala's factory is the companion object: an apply method acts as a factory method (the Scala book says so explicitly) and Order(...) is sugar for it, so the classic factory class is never written, while a private constructor plus a make/from returning Either or Option is the established smart-constructor idiom. The compile-time path and the runtime path can be split with inline def plus scala.compiletime.error for literal arguments and a from method for runtime values. Use Either for a single failure, cats Validated when all invalid fields must be reported together, and Scala 3 opaque types when the underlying type must be invisible so the companion's smart constructor is the only door.
pitfalls: A case class keeps a public copy even with a private constructor, so callers can clone an instance while skipping validation; use a regular class for strict invariants.
Either-based factories short-circuit on the first error; switch to Validated/NonEmptyChain when the caller needs every invalid field at once.
Throwing from apply hides failure in the type; return Option/Either/Validated for expected invalid input.

variants.name: Opaque type with inline compile-time validation (Scala 3)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 opaque types make the representation invisible outside the defining scope, so the companion's apply/from pair becomes the only possible way to obtain a value: an inline apply validates literal arguments at compile time (scala.compiletime.error) and a from method returns Either for runtime input. Choose this when a wrong input should be a compile error where possible and an explicit error value otherwise, not a runtime exception.
pitfalls: Opaque types are transparent inside the file/object that defines them; helper code in the same scope can still construct values without validation.
Extension methods must be provided for every operation clients need, otherwise the factory forces callers to unwrap via a public conversion and the abstraction leaks.
inline validation only works on constant expressions; runtime values silently take the from path, so both paths must enforce the same rule.
